subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Verify Rolle's theorem for the function log(x² + 2) − log 3 on (−1, 1).

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say why the function is defined everywhere, and how you get c.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Check the conditions on [−1, 1]
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that x² + 2 > 0 for every real x — that line shows that f is continuous and differentiable for every real x. The interval is read as the closed interval [−1, 1], since the endpoint values are needed.
steps.memory_tip: x² is never negative, so x² + 2 is never below 2 and the logarithm is defined for every real x.
lines: x² ≥ 0 for every real x, so x² + 2 ≥ 2 > 0
and the logarithm is defined for every real x
(log u is continuous and differentiable where u > 0,

lines.text: and here u = x² + 2 > 0 for every x)

lines: (i) f is continuous on the closed interval [−1, 1]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (−1, 1)
and  f(1) = log(1 + 2) − log 3 = log 3 − log 3 = 0
∴ f(−1) = f(1) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies.

recall.must_convey: That x² + 2 > 0 for every real x, so f is continuous on [−1, 1] and differentiable on (−1, 1), and that f(−1) = f(1) = 0.
accept: x squared plus two is always at least two so the log is always defined
both ends give log three minus log three which is zero
the function is continuous and differentiable for every real x
x square plus two eppudu positive kabatti log define avuthundi
there is no point to exclude from the domain

steps.why: A logarithm is continuous only where the expression inside it is positive, so that has to be settled first. Here x² + 2 is at least 2 for every real x, so there is no point to exclude and the first two conditions hold for every real x.
common_mistakes: Excluding points where x² + 2 = 0, an equation with no real solution.
Reading log(x² + 2) − log 3 as log(x² + 2 − 3) instead of a difference of two logarithms.

steps.label: Solve f′(c) = 0 inside (−1, 1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. log 3 is a constant, so it differentiates to 0 and only log(x² + 2) contributes. The chain rule supplies the 2x on top.
steps.memory_tip: The derivative of log u is u′/u, so the numerator carries the derivative of the expression inside.

lines.text: (chain rule: d/dx of log u is (1/u) · du/dx with
u = x² + 2; log 3 is a constant)

lines: c² + 2 is never 0, so the fraction is 0 only
−1 < 0 < 1, so c = 0 lies in the open interval (−1, 1)

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = 0 ∈ (−1, 1)

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 2x/(x² + 2), that the denominator is never zero so only 2c = 0 matters, and that c = 0 lies in (−1, 1).
accept: the derivative is two x over x squared plus two
the denominator is never zero so set the numerator to zero
two c equals zero so c is zero, which is inside the interval
numerator zero pettina c zero vasthundi
log three is a constant so it differentiates to zero

steps.why: A fraction is zero only where its numerator is zero and its denominator is not, so saying that c² + 2 can never vanish is what makes c = 0 the only root. Here log is the natural logarithm; with any other base the derivative is multiplied by a constant factor, so c = 0 in either case.
common_mistakes: Differentiating log(x² + 2) as 1/(x² + 2) and leaving out the factor 2x from the chain rule.
Differentiating the constant log 3 to 1/3 instead of 0.
Setting the denominator to zero as well and inventing extra roots.
lines_compact: c² + 2 is never 0, so the fraction is 0 only
−1 < 0 < 1, so c = 0 lies in the open interval (−1, 1)

lines_compact.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = 0 ∈ (−1, 1)

insider_note: x² + 2 is never zero, so the logarithm is defined everywhere and continuity is easy to argue. The −log 3 is a constant and vanishes on differentiating.
